title: No closed fist
hookLine: the Buddha, ill, says there is no teacher's closed fist: nothing held back
carry: an open hand in both directions

cards: The rains are about to begin. The Buddha sends the monks off to spend the season around Vesali, wherever they have friends, and stays on with Ananda in the little village of Beluva.
Then the illness comes, sharp and dangerous. Ananda watches, frightened, and holds on to one hope. Surely the teacher won't go without some last word for the community.
Something kept for the end, saved for the people closest to him.

teach.b: The sickness is severe. The Mahaparinibbana Sutta says sharp pains came on him, close to death, and he bore them mindfully, without complaint.
He thinks it wouldn't be right to pass away without speaking to the community, so he pushes the illness back by effort and recovers for a while.
Then he sits in the shade, and Ananda comes and confesses how frightened he was. I took a little comfort, he says, in thinking you wouldn't go without leaving some instruction about the community.
And the Buddha answers: what does the community expect of me, Ananda?
I have taught the Dhamma without making any inside and outside.
In the Pali, the Tathagata has no acariya-mutthi, no teacher's closed fist, holding something back for the end. Everything has already been given. Then he adds something just as surprising.
He has never thought, I lead the community, or the community depends on me. So why would he need to leave instructions about leading it? And then, a picture of himself.
I am old now, Ananda, eighty years old.

teach.h: AN OLD CART HELD WITH STRAPS.
teach.b: Like an old cart kept going by being held together with straps, this body keeps going only by being held together. Two kinds of honesty in one scene. Nothing hidden about the teaching.
Nothing hidden about the body either.
The fist is open in both directions: here is everything I know, and here is how frail I am. A teacher could easily guard a secret, or a reputation. This one opens his hand.

how: Buddhist teachers often cite the open hand of DN 16 when they say there is no secret core held back for insiders, and Theravada communities chant and teach the suttas openly to anyone who comes.

o: a teacher's blessing given at the end
a secret teaching for the closest pupils
a teacher's closed fist, holding back

games.q: no closed fist: tap the pairs.
p: a last instruction about the community

s: the Buddha saved a secret teaching for Ananda at the end
he says he taught without inside or outside, with no closed fist.
the Buddha says he never thought of himself as leading the community
so he sees no need to leave instructions about leading it.
the Buddha compares his body to an old cart held together with straps
he says he is eighty, and the body keeps going only by being held together.

games.q: you're Ananda. the Buddha has recovered from a terrible illness. you tell him you hoped for a final instruction about the community. what does he say?
o: he says he held nothing back and never thought of himself as the community's leader.
he gives Ananda a secret teaching.
games.why: no closed fist: everything has been taught, and he never thought the community depended on him.

practice: Make a loose fist with one hand and feel the effort it takes to hold it closed. Then slowly let the fingers open, until the hand rests palm up on your knee.
With the hand open, notice whether there's something you've been holding back from someone: a piece of knowledge, a skill, an honest word, or the plain fact that you're tired.

wordCard.voice: Acariyamutthi. The Buddha's words at Beluva: there is nothing kept back, no secret teaching saved for the end. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali acariyamutthi: acariya, teacher; mutthi, fist. the closed fist the Buddha says he never had.

carryVoice: Your line: an open hand in both directions. Nothing hidden in the teaching, and nothing hidden about his frailty. Day five hundred forty-seven, done.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), the illness at Beluva and the closed fist
